query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of yttrium (≈0.5 at%) to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will induce the in‐situ formation of a stable, lubricious oxide phase during sliding that maintains low friction and wear rates over the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with typical high-temperature oxidation and wear behavior, showing acceptable low-friction performance only at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 0.5 atomic percent yttrium into the alloy composition during melting and solidification.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed in air under moderate loads, with operating temperatures ranging from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The yttrium addition is expected to segregate to grain boundaries and sliding interfaces, promoting the nucleation and growth of a thin, discontinuous yttrium-rich oxide film (e.g., Y2O3 or Y-containing complex oxides) during sliding.
generation.mechanism: Under tribological conditions, the reactive yttrium additive oxidizes preferentially to form a stable, low-shear-strength oxide film on the sliding surface. This tribo-oxide acts as a solid lubricant, reducing coefficient of friction and wear even as the temperature increases. The oxide film also serves to protect the underlying matrix from severe mechanical degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the yttrium-modified alloy will exhibit consistently lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates over the entire temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C).
generation.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which typically shows increased friction and wear at elevated temperatures due to uncontrolled oxidation and microstructural degradation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under oxidizing (air) environments, moderate loading conditions, and for temperatures spanning from ambient to 800 °C. Performance outside these conditions (e.g., high vacuum, extreme loads) has not been addressed.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise stability, thickness, and adherence of the yttrium-induced oxide film over prolonged sliding and under variable loads. Additional uncertainty exists about the impact of yttrium on other mechanical properties of the alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the standard CoCrFeNi alloy and another set with 0.5 at% yttrium addition. Conduct controlled sliding wear experiments in air across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under identical moderate load conditions. Compare surface morphology (using SEM/EDS), friction coefficients (via tribometer measurements), and wear rates (using profilometry) for both sample sets.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature
Wear rate (mass loss or volume loss) at each temperature interval
Surface oxide composition and morphology post-sliding (using XRD/SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-modified samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficients and wear rates compared to the baseline alloy under the same test conditions, or if the anticipated stable, lubricious oxide film is absent from the worn surfaces, then the hypothesis would be falsified.
